links.site_note: No campaign website found (The Ballot Brief, Sept 15, 2026; Ballotpedia; iVoterGuide).

oneliner.t: Palmer Republican and perennial candidate who calls himself a 'constitutional Christian conservative' and runs to Sen. Sullivan's right; he finished fifth in the primary (1.1%) and moved onto the November ballot when fourth-place Democrat David Leslie withdrew.

upbringing.t: Little is documented. ADN (2024) reports he is a minister at an Anchorage church and says he first ran for governor in 2006 because he felt called by God; Ballotpedia, citing his own interview answers, says he served in the Alaska Air National Guard; Wikipedia's race page describes him as a bassist. Age, birthplace and education were not found.

platform.t: Supports a total, nationwide abortion ban, including in cases of rape and incest (2024); Ballotpedia's summary of a 2024 interview also records him saying abortion and contraception should be left to states, so his stated positions are not consistent.
Wants more state authority and less federal control; opposes congressionally directed spending (earmarks).
Backs more oil, gas and coal production, criticizes EPA rules and is skeptical of climate change as a policy concern.
Stronger border enforcement, fiscal restraint, strong support for Israel; opposes transgender participation in women's sports and restrooms.
Says he does not rank other candidates: 'It's a one-shot deal.'

record.t: Ballotpedia's race list starts in 2014; a 2006 candidacy was not confirmed from election records. The FEC lists him in a 2008 Senate cycle with no financial data.

claims.claim: Served in the Alaska Air National Guard.
Is a minister at an Anchorage church.

record.t: Church not named; not independently confirmed.

claims.claim: Has run repeatedly for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House.

record.t: Ballotpedia lists governor primaries 2014 (3.6%) and 2018 (0.7%) and U.S. House runs in 2016 (5.2%), 2020 (5.8%) and 2024 (0.4%); FEC lists a 2008 Senate candidacy; iVoterGuide also lists 2016/2020/2024 House races.

aipac_endorse.t: No AIPAC endorsement found; not listed on Track AIPAC's candidates page (as of 2026-10-08).

statements.t: Expressed strong support for Israel in a 2024 Alaska Beacon interview (as summarized by Ballotpedia).

support: Right For Alaska (super PAC, Hudson, Wis.) — about $410,000 promoting him (Jul 30–Aug 7, 2026; OpenSecrets). Its ads said he was more conservative and more anti-abortion than Sullivan, as part of a strategy reported as aimed at weakening Sullivan. ADN later put its pro-Heikes spending at 'more than $400,000'.

fec.outside_note: Right For Alaska also spent ~$574,000 against Sen. Sullivan and ~$219,000 for Alaskan Party candidate Skip Southworth (OpenSecrets, through Aug 7). The NYT (via Election Law Blog) and Alaska Public Media describe it as a long-shot-boosting effort; Alaska Public Media reports its only disclosed donor at that point was William Harris of Lexington, Mass. ($100,000), a frequent donor to Democrats who support abortion rights.

history.note: Cycle listed on FEC; no financial data shown.
Ballotpedia reports no contributions for 2020 or 2024. FEC IDs for the House runs not found.
FEC has no 2025–26 reports for him (likely under the $5,000 filing threshold; not confirmed).

money_flags_note: No corporate or foreign-policy-lobby money to his campaign found. Right For Alaska, which spent for him, reported $1,285,000 from party committees, $990,000 from other committees and $100,000 from individuals through Sep 30, 2026 (FEC summary). The committee names were not visible, so whether any corporate money is involved is unknown.

donors: Party committees (names not shown on FEC summary)
superpac_donors.note: Formed Mar 23, 2026; treasurer Thomas Datwyler. Total receipts $2,375,017 and independent expenditures $2,353,093 through Sep 30, 2026. 'spent' is the pro-Heikes portion through Aug 7 only.

note.t: No financial disclosure found or searched.

democracy_note: Never held office. No statements on the 2020/2024 results found (not specifically searched).

access.note: Did not answer the Alaska Beacon questionnaire (listed there as 'withdrawn', which conflicts with his certified ballot status; probably stale). Told ADN he would be 'doing interviews in a couple of weeks' after advancing.

note.t: Palmer resident; has run in Alaska races since at least 2008 (FEC) or 2006 (his account).

history_2024.t: In the 2024 U.S. House primary, Vote Alaska Before Party, a Democrat-backed group run by consultant Jim Lottsfeldt, spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on ads highlighting his support for a nationwide abortion ban, as part of nearly $1M also aimed at Republicans Dahlstrom and Begich. He got 0.4%.

checks.legal: No CourtListener/Justia or Alaska CourtView searches run. News reviewed (ADN 2024, Alaska Current, Beacon, OpenSecrets) mentions no legal matters.
checks.claims: No campaign website, ads or questionnaire answers exist. Sample = his own statements in the 2024 ADN interview and Ballotpedia's summary of his 2024 Beacon interview: 4 bio claims (1 true, 3 unverifiable); his issue statements are positions, not checkable facts. Fewer than 5 checkable claims are available.
checks.democracy: Not specifically searched; never held office.

recordx.note: Not an officeholder; no FEC committee activity reported for 2025–26.

research_notes: Primary: 1,641 votes, 1.12% on the unofficial Aug 25 printout (fourth, 27 votes ahead of Leslie); ADN says that after certification he finished 109 votes behind Leslie, so he placed fifth and advanced only when Leslie withdrew on Aug 31. Sources conflict on the order before certification; certified totals were not opened. Right For Alaska: FEC shows $1.285M from 'party committees' through Sep 30 while OpenSecrets (Aug 12) named only Harris. The party committees' identities need a human check on FEC Schedule A. Reporting describes the pro-Heikes spending as a strategy to pull votes from Sullivan, not as support from Heikes, and nothing documents coordination with him. He did not respond to OpenSecrets.
